assessmentSummary.identity: One Short Foot to Calf Raise repetition is performed from a bilateral standing base. Start with both heels, first metatarsal heads, fifth metatarsal heads, and relaxed long toes supported on a clean dry level surface. Gently create a short-foot arch on both feet by drawing the metatarsal heads toward the heels without curling or lifting the toes. Maintain the forefoot contacts while rising directly upward into a comfortable bilateral heel raise, pause only as prescribed, lower both heels with control to the same flat-foot start, then fully relax the short-foot action before the next repetition. The heel is expected to leave contact during the rise; first and fifth metatarsal head contact and quiet toe behavior remain required. Standing hands-free and light wall-touch are exact variants. Single-leg, step, seated, bent-knee, externally loaded, sustained-top-hold, rebound, toe-dorsiflexed, manually assisted, resistance-on-midfoot, or clinical treatment forms change the variant or definition.
currentCardFindings: Source 877 has one stable legacy definition but its source variant does not define the ordered arch-to-rise-to-lower-to-release sequence, the fact that heel contact intentionally changes, support variants, dose, fatigue, substitutions, or review state.

The compound sequence is distinct from standalone Short-Foot Drill and Standing Calf Raise. The arch set precedes the bilateral plantarflexion cycle; it is not a claim of universal arch behavior or clinical outcome.
Five legacy candidates returned healthy oEmbed metadata. At least one title signals a single-leg form, so all remain candidate-only and require exact-variant matching before use.
assessmentSummary.programmingDecision: Select only when the exact bilateral support variant, clean visible foot-safe surface, arch-set quality, comfortable calf-raise range, symptoms, restrictions, planned dose, duration, logistics, and cumulative foot, toe, calf, Achilles, balance, running, landing, jumping, agility, and lower-body budgets fit. Do not silently substitute standalone short-foot, ordinary calf raise, single-leg, step, seated, bent-knee, loaded, held, rebound, or clinical forms. Recompute selection, fatigue, impact, duration, logistics, substitutions, persistence, and coach and athlete rendering after every change.

calibrationEvidence.basis: Direct short-foot mechanics, double-leg heel-raise mechanics and muscle-activity studies, direct arch-raise-with-heel-raise evidence used only as adjacent support, a foot-core clinical sequence used only for ordered cueing, general exercise safeguards, Source 877 context, five oEmbed records, and comparison with Short-Foot Drill, Standing Calf Raise, Big Toe Press Iso Hold, and Single-Leg Tripod Balance.
calibrationEvidence.uncertainty: No source establishes a universal arch height, heel-raise range, tempo, dose, recovery interval, transfer, participant threshold, or Vortex score. The resisted arch-raise study is not treated as equivalent to this unresisted card. No video, relationship, score, or publication is approved.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Stand with both heels, first metatarsal heads, fifth metatarsal heads, and relaxed long toes supported on a clean dry level surface. Gently shorten both feet by drawing the metatarsal heads toward the heels without curling or lifting the toes. Keep forefoot contacts while rising directly upward into a comfortable bilateral calf raise, lower both heels with control to the same flat-foot start, then fully relax the arch set before the next repetition. The heels intentionally leave contact during the rise; first and fifth metatarsal head contact and quiet toe behavior remain required. Hands-free and light wall-touch are exact variants.

evidence.sourceTitle: Non-Operative Management of Symptomatic Hallux Limitus: A Novel Approach of Foot Core Stabilization and Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: The clinical sequence describes activating the arch before slowly rising on the toes.
Vortex defines an unresisted bilateral short-foot set followed by rise, controlled lower, and full release; it does not adopt clinical treatment claims.

evidence.sourceTitle: The influence of body posture and added mass on intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscle activation and force output during common foot strengthening exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Short-foot and double-leg heel-raise tasks are separately described in the study protocol.
The card is an ordered compound sequence, distinct from either standalone exercise.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic examination of a new exercise therapy for the intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscles
claims: The arch-raise study measured intrinsic and extrinsic foot and lower-leg muscle activity during arch raise, short foot, and heel raise tasks.
The card records contributors and joint actions without claiming isolated muscles or equivalence to a resisted arch-raise protocol.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic Assessment of the Lower Leg Muscles during Concentric and Eccentric Phases of Standing Heel Raise
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
claims: Standing heel raises have distinct concentric and eccentric phases.
Vortex requires an arch set before the rise, retained forefoot contacts while heels lift, controlled lowering, and a complete release before the next repetition.

evidence.sourceTitle: Relationship of Physical Factors to the Acceptability and Unacceptability of Short Foot Exercise: A Preliminary Study
claims: Short-foot execution can be technically difficult even before a standing compound task is added.
Candidate scores describe the compound task's complexity and physical demand only; they do not classify people.

evidence.sourceTitle: Comparison of ankle plantar flexor activity between double-leg heel raise and walking
claims: Double-leg heel raise produces plantar-flexor activity distinct from walking.
Vortex treats this as a bodyweight calf and foot exposure and tracks valid repetitions, range, support, faults, symptoms, and overlapping lower-leg demand; recovery remains a planning estimate.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Safe supervised exercise requires appropriate instruction, progression, environment, and technique control.
Vortex requires a clean dry level surface, foot visibility, selected support, space, hygiene, communication, and exit conditions without demographic classification.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic Assessment of the Lower Leg Muscles during Concentric and Eccentric Phases of Standing Heel Raise
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
claims: The study examined phase-specific activity rather than one universal workout prescription.
Candidate repetition, tempo, and rest ranges remain quarantined and stop before arch, forefoot, body, or symptom quality degrades.

evidence.sourceTitle: Non-Operative Management of Symptomatic Hallux Limitus: A Novel Approach of Foot Core Stabilization and Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy
evidence.sourcePublisher: International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
claims: The source cues arch activation followed by slow rise on the toes.
Vortex adds bilateral start and return contacts, the intentional heel lift boundary, controlled lower, full release, and valid repetition rules.

evidence.sourceTitle: Achilles Tendon Loading During Heel-Raising and -Lowering Exercises
claims: Heel-raising and lowering exercises load the Achilles tendon and were performed with explicit range and support criteria.
Stop for pain, instability, symptom escalation, lost forefoot contacts, toe curl, unsafe station, or inability to restore controlled rise and lower; do not use this card as an Achilles protocol.

evidence.sourceTitle: Evidence for Intrinsic Foot Muscle Training in Improving Foot Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
claims: Intrinsic-foot programs are heterogeneous in exercise and dosage.
The compound may serve preparation or resilience only when purpose, calf and foot recovery, and later high-output lower-body work fit; no universal outcome is promised.

evidence.sourceTitle: Reliability of doming and toe flexion testing to quantify foot muscle strength
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Foot and Ankle Research
claims: Short-foot mechanics use forefoot-to-heel shortening with toe and heel contact criteria.
Athlete support uses a gentle arch set, quiet long toes, direct-up heel rise, slow lower, full relax, and no-chasing-fatigue cue.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic Assessment of the Lower Leg Muscles during Concentric and Eccentric Phases of Standing Heel Raise
evidence.sourcePublisher: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
claims: Standing heel raise phases can be distinguished for observation.
Coaches record support, arch set, toe behavior, forefoot contact, heel path, range, lower control, release, first fault, symptoms, and actual exposure without diagnosing impairment.

evidence.sourceTitle: Youth Resistance Training: Updated Position Statement Paper From the NSCA
claims: Task selection and progression should account for the exact exercise, environment, instruction, and supervision.
Wall-touch, smaller range, fewer repetitions, slower cadence, more rest, captions, stills, transcript, and live instruction can improve access while preserving the exact bilateral sequence.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic examination of a new exercise therapy for the intrinsic and extrinsic foot muscles
claims: Arch raise, short foot, and heel raise are distinct task conditions in the study.
The unresisted compound card is not silently merged with resisted arch raise, standalone short-foot, ordinary heel raise, single-leg, step, or seated forms.
YouTube supports embedded playback subject to video and platform state.
Five candidates returned healthy YouTube oEmbed metadata on 2026-08-09; exact bilateral sequence, support, captions, accessibility, safety, and approval remain unverified.
